newsitem.title: UK: Britain's Major taunted over legislation defeat.
newsitem.headline: Britain's Major taunted over legislation defeat.

text.p: British Prime Minister John Major on Tuesday shrugged off a surprise defeat in parliament as a miscount and said it would not change his tactics ahead of a general election due by May.
But opposition Labour Party leader Tony Blair taunted Major, accusing him of being desperate to hold on to power.
"Why doesn't the prime minister call a halt to what is...a tired out government?" Blair told parliament.
"If they're so confident why doesn't the prime minister just for once stop the dithering, name the day and call an election," he added to cheers from members of his party.

The opposition took advantage of ministers being away at a cabinet brainstorming session at the prime minister's country residence on Monday to stage a late-night ambush in the House of Commons, the lower chamber of parliament, over government education plans.
Labour claimed a knife-edge victory with 273 votes to the government's 272. If all MPs are in parliament, the ruling Conservatives and the combined opposition have 322 votes each.
Major, accusing Labour of "student union" politics, said he understood the government had not been defeated. Education Secretary Gillian Shephard said earlier there had been a miscount.

"We understand that last night the vote was in fact a tie, which under the procedures of the House (of Commons) would have meant that the government didn't lose it, because in those circumstances the Speaker...votes with the government," said Shephard.
Labour said it was not clear what had happened but, under parliamentary rules, the result must stand.
Labour's senior parliamentary business manager, Donald Dewar, said there was a discrepancy between the count of people passing through voting lobbies and the names recorded on a list.

"Whatever happened...it is further evidence of the confusion and chaos which is now surrounding activities in the House of Commons. The reason for that is that the government...is without purpose and simply hanging on and hoping," he said.
The government has said it will reinstate the plans -- to let schools which have opted out of local authority control expand -- as the Education Bill goes through parliament.
Major used the brainstorming session on Monday to reaffirm that his favoured date for the election is May 1, almost at the end of his government's maximum allotted term of office.
The Conservatives have been in office for 18 consecutive years but opinion polls show they are 20 points behind Labour.
Monday night's vote proved how difficult Labour can make it for the government to keep the upper hand in parliament as the days tick away to the election.
